description: Lindsey Buckingham's breakup letter to Stevie Nicks, sung with Nicks harmonising right beside him. The lead single from Rumours became Fleetwood Mac's first US Top 10 hit — rock's sunniest-sounding goodbye.

pops.text: Buckingham wrote this at a house the band rented in Florida between tour legs. It was the first song he presented for Rumours — Mick Fleetwood said the house had a haunted, bad-vibe feel.

It's a breakup song aimed at bandmate Stevie Nicks, written, in Buckingham's words, as a stream of consciousness. Nicks later called her own 'Dreams' and this song 'counter songs' about the same split.
Producer Ken Caillat nearly wrote it off at the demo stage: Buckingham was beating his acoustic guitar as hard as he could and screaming, and Caillat thought it sounded completely non-musical.

That galloping drum groove was inspired by the Rolling Stones' 'Street Fighting Man.' Buckingham demonstrated it with air tom fills, hair flying, and Fleetwood turned it into his own tom-tom variation.
Nothing here was played together: the track was built from overdubs across three separate studios over four months. That piecemeal method was the Rumours way.
The guitar solo is a stitch job. Caillat came back from a Christmas break in Lake Tahoe and assembled it from six different lead takes, riding faders to mute and unmute each fragment.

Nicks asked Buckingham to cut the line 'packing up, shacking up is all you wanna do' — she insisted it wasn't true. He kept it, and she said every time it came up onstage she wanted to go over and kill him.
It was released on 20 December 1976 because the band wanted a US single out by Christmas, ahead of the album. Rumours pre-orders hit 800,000 — then the largest advance sale in Warner Bros. history.
It peaked at No. 10 on the Billboard Hot 100 in March 1977, held there for two weeks, and became the band's first US Top 10 hit. In the UK it initially stalled at No. 38.
Rolling Stone ranked it No. 1 on its list of Fleetwood Mac's 50 greatest songs. Not bad for a song its producer first heard as a man shouting over a battered acoustic guitar.

title: Go Your Own Way

description: INXS bet on themselves, paid for this session out of their own pocket, and won a worldwide record deal with it. A slinky new-wave calling card that became their first US Top 40 hit, helped by a banquet video MTV loved.

pops.text: In January 1982 INXS toured New Zealand supporting Cold Chisel, and manager Chris Murphy decided their label, Deluxe, wasn't their future. Deluxe had failed to attract any international interest.
So the band paid to record this song themselves, with producer Mark Opitz at Paradise Studios in Sydney. It turned out so well that Murphy hired Opitz to produce three more songs.
Written by Michael Hutchence and Andrew Farriss, it was released in July 1982 as the first single from the band's third album, Shabooh Shoobah, which followed that October.
The single did the negotiating: Murphy took it to WEA, and in July 1982 INXS signed fresh deals — WEA for Australia and Asia, Atco for North America and PolyGram for Europe and the UK.
At home it peaked at No. 14 on the Australian Kent Music Report chart. It was also nominated for Best Australian Single at the 1982 Countdown Music Awards.
The video, directed by Soren Jensen, cuts between the band performing and a decadent banquet with models — including Hutchence's then-girlfriend, Michele Bennett.

Two of those models, Susan Stenmark and Karen Pini, were actresses on the soap The Young Doctors. Jensen had been an assistant director on the show, and Hutchence knew him through his mother Patricia, its make-up artist.

Guitarist Tim Farriss remembered the shoot fondly: cats roaming the banquet table, the band ripping apart a turkey with models and Playboy centerfolds. 'Next thing we knew we had a top 40 hit in America and were opening for Adam Ant.'
This was the first INXS video to air on the fledgling MTV, and it went into high rotation. The band credit that exposure with a big share of the single's US success.
In May–June 1983 it reached No. 30 on the Billboard Hot 100 — INXS's first US Top 40 hit. On album-rock radio it went even bigger, peaking at No. 2 on Billboard's Top Tracks chart.

title: The One Thing

description: A waltz-time power ballad Andrew Farriss first sketched as a bluesy piano demo and Michael Hutchence turned into a love lyric for Michele Bennett. Kick's fourth single, and now — officially — Australia's favourite song.

pops.text: Andrew Farriss started the chords on an upright piano while INXS were on a world tour in 1986. He recorded a blues-style demo and handed it to Michael Hutchence, who came back with the lyric.
The demo was a piano blues in the style of Fats Domino. Producer Chris Thomas suggested a synth-based arrangement instead, replacing the piano part with sweeping synthesised strings.

Hutchence wrote the words for his then-girlfriend Michele Bennett, described as his first real love. Fittingly, it was Bennett who had introduced Hutchence to Richard Lowenstein, the director of this video.
Underneath the drama, it's a waltz: the song moves in the tempo of a modern Viennese waltz, layered with synths and dramatic pauses before Kirk Pengilly's saxophone solo near the end.
Released in June 1988 as the fourth single from Kick, it peaked at No. 7 on the Billboard Hot 100. Its original peaks elsewhere were more modest: No. 24 in the UK and No. 14 in Australia.
The video, with an extended intro, was filmed in Prague by Richard Lowenstein — on the same trip he also shot the videos for 'Guns in the Sky' and 'New Sensation.'
At the 1989 ARIA Music Awards the song was nominated for four awards and won two: Best Group, and Best Video for Lowenstein's Prague clip.
After Hutchence's death in 1997, his coffin was carried out of St Andrew's Cathedral in Sydney by his bandmates and his brother Rhett — with this song playing in the background.
Since March 2014, AFL club Port Adelaide has used it as its unofficial pre-match anthem at Adelaide Oval. Fans raise scarves above their heads and sing it before the opening bounce.
In July 2025, listeners voted it 'The Best Australian Song of All Time' in Triple J's Hottest 100 of Australian Songs — with the biggest share of its votes coming from 18-to-29-year-olds.

title: Never Tear Us Apart

description: Kick's two-minute rhyme machine, welded straight onto the end of 'Need You Tonight.' Andrew Farriss rhymes nearly every line with '-ate,' then the band salutes Bob Dylan with cue cards, deliberate typos and a sax solo.

pops.text: On Kick, this song segues directly out of 'Need You Tonight' with no gap — which is why the two are so often heard, and were first filmed, as one continuous piece.
Its party trick is in the title: almost every line rhymes with the word 'ate.' Mediate, deviate, depreciate — Farriss keeps the chain running for the whole song.

The writing credit came from a swap. Hutchence helped Farriss with these lyrics, Farriss helped Hutchence with 'Guns in the Sky' — so each man took sole credit on one song: Farriss here, Hutchence there.
It was never released as a single in its original form. It got a video anyway, tucked onto the end of the 'Need You Tonight' clip — two songs promoted for the price of one.
That video is a tribute to Bob Dylan's 'Subterranean Homesick Blues' clip: the band flips cue cards bearing the lyrics, and the final card reads 'Sax Solo,' cueing Kirk Pengilly's soprano sax.
Even the mistakes are faithful to Dylan: the cue cards contain spelling errors, including 'Facinate' for 'Fascinate,' echoing the sloppy cards in Dylan's original film.

One card rewards a pause: under the line 'a special date' sits '9-8-1945.' In Australian day-first format that's 9 August 1945, the date of the Nagasaki atomic bombing — not 8 September, as US viewers sometimes read it.
The cue-card sequence was filmed somewhere suitably industrial: near blast furnace number 6 at the Port Kembla Steelworks in New South Wales, Australia.
The combined 'Need You Tonight / Mediate' video won five MTV Video Music Awards, including Video of the Year. A two-minute album track had just helped win the biggest video prize going.

It finally became a single decades later: INXS re-recorded it with Tricky on vocals for the 2010 album Original Sin, and Ralphi Rosario's remixes peaked at No. 5 on Billboard's dance chart in September 2011.

title: Mediate

description: The Brooklyn trio's lead single from A Way Forward: five minutes of motorik rush about the exact moment a friendship tips into something more. Guitar-forward, propulsive and joyously panicked — exactly as intended.

pops.text: Released on 3 June 2021, this was the first single from the band's second album, A Way Forward — the album itself was announced the same day and arrived on 5 November 2021.
Songwriter Ian Devaney says it's about the moment a non-romantic relationship flips into something different: 'the air in the room suddenly feels like it changes in an undefinable way.'
Devaney called it a celebration of 'that certain joyous panic.' Sonically, he wanted it to feel like running down a hill, just out of control.
That downhill energy came from listening to Thee Oh Sees, and admiring how they supercharge krautrock rhythms with a kind of mania. Devaney set out to make that vibe the band's own.
It was a deliberate door-opener: Devaney placed it second on the album, after an introductory track, and noted it has more guitar than any Nation of Language song before it.
The title line nearly went somewhere darker. Devaney weighed writing about fun or about addiction, then decided the music was far too peppy to back an addiction song.
This track was produced and mixed by Abe Seiferth, who also worked on the band's debut, and mastered by Heba Kadry — production across the album was split with Nick Milhiser of Holy Ghost!
There's no glossy video shoot here: the official lyric video was filmed and edited by Nation of Language themselves.
At 5 minutes 25 seconds, it's the longest track on A Way Forward. The album was recorded during the 2020 lockdowns, digging into Kraftwerk, Neu! and other 1970s electronic pioneers.
In January 2022 this was the song Nation of Language chose for their television debut, performing it on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert.

title: Across That Fine Line

description: The third single from Dance Called Memory, Nation of Language's 2025 Sub Pop debut — a minimalist, oscillating-synth swoon that frontman Ian Devaney nearly left off the album entirely.

pops.text: This was the third single from Dance Called Memory, released July 22, 2025 — ahead of the album's September 19 arrival.
Nation of Language are a Brooklyn trio: Ian Devaney on vocals and guitar, Aidan Noell on synths, and Alex MacKay on bass.
Devaney started the band after hearing OMD's 'Electricity' in his father's car — a childhood favourite that sent him off fooling around on a keyboard.
Dance Called Memory is the band's fourth album, and their full-length debut for Sub Pop Records.
Producer Nick Millhiser of Holy Ghost! returned after making Strange Disciple with them, and Heba Kadry mastered the record in Brooklyn.
Hear that oscillating synth pulse? One reviewer heard a nod to Kraftwerk — though Devaney says this album leans toward Brian Eno's more human school of synth music.
This song almost missed the album entirely. The band had already turned in the final mixes for mastering when its fate was decided.
The deadline was real: they were about to leave for a January tour of Australia supporting IDLES.
Devaney says clarity struck somewhere over the Pacific Ocean, while he was sequencing the album mid-flight — 'Under the Water' made the cut.
Weeks before the album dropped, the band played this song live in KEXP's Seattle studio — that session was recorded August 4, 2025.

title: Under the Water

description: Track two on Dance Called Memory (2025), where Devaney's sad, lilting demo got rebuilt around relentless electronic percussion — every drum smashed through a synthesizer.

pops.text: This is track two on Dance Called Memory, Nation of Language's fourth album, released September 19, 2025.
Devaney brought this song into the studio as something much more sad and lilting in nature. It did not stay that way.
Producer Nick Millhiser reached for Radiohead's 'Idioteque' as a reference point, adding a relentless, almost-'90s electronic percussion drive.
Every bit of percussion on this track was smashed through a synthesizer — the band's way of casting a shade of early-2000s electronic music.
That burbling bassline had reviewers reaching for a comparison: Peter Hook, of Joy Division and New Order fame.
The album around it is about loss and change — and, in Devaney's words, how quickly those things pile up faster than you're ready for.
Devaney and synth player Aidan Noell are married — the couple once swapped a traditional wedding registry for funds toward their second album.
Bassist Alex MacKay joined in 2022, replacing Michael Sue-Poi — Devaney's bandmate from their earlier group, The Static Jacks.
The band road-tested it early: this song opened their World Cafe studio session for NPR, recorded in Philadelphia.
During the band's three-night album-release run at Warsaw in Brooklyn, this one turned up in an encore.

title: In Another Life

description: The opening track of Smokers Delight (1995), Nightmares on Wax's downtempo landmark — a 4:40 haze built on Quincy Jones's 'Summer in the City,' with a wistful vocal about leaving home.

pops.text: This opens Smokers Delight, released September 25, 1995 on Warp Records — Nightmares on Wax's second album.
That lush groove is built on Quincy Jones's version of 'Summer in the City' — the album's own credits note the sample.
The song underneath started with the Lovin' Spoonful in the mid-'60s; its writers, John Sebastian, Mark Sebastian and Steve Boone, share the credit here.
Quincy Jones's 1973 arrangement of it won the Grammy for Best Instrumental Arrangement — prime sampling material, then.
Full circle: George Evelyn's father and sister introduced him to Quincy Jones's music when he was a kid in Leeds.
Yes, that's a real vocal drifting by — a homesick reverie about coffee tables, rain-streaked windows and everybody leaving home.
This track was recorded at FON Studios in Sheffield, according to the album's credits — other tracks were cut in Wakefield.
By this album, co-founder Kevin 'Boywonder' Harper had left; Evelyn carried on, joined by keyboardist Robin Taylor-Firth.
The album title answers the Sugarhill Gang's 'Rapper's Delight' — same delight, served considerably slower.
Fact magazine later ranked Smokers Delight at No. 15 on its list of the 50 Best Trip-Hop Albums of All Time.

title: Nights Introlude

description: A fan favourite from In a Space Outta Sound (2006), built on a 1968 Stax duet and assembled in about two hours — later reborn at Abbey Road with a gospel choir, strings and horns.

pops.text: This is track six on In a Space Outta Sound, Nightmares on Wax's fifth studio album, released on Warp in March 2006.
That warm soul loop is 'Private Number,' a 1968 Stax duet by Judy Clay and William Bell.
'Private Number' carries writing credits for William Bell and Booker T. Jones — and both names ride along in this track's credits, too.
The sample first lived in a song Evelyn wrote for singer Mozez. When that didn't click, he pulled it out and kept it for himself.
Keyboardist Robin Taylor-Firth re-phrased the guitar loop and jammed around it — three takes, which Evelyn then chopped up.
Unusually for a producer who obsesses over details, 'You Wish' came together in under two hours.
The official video sends George Evelyn wandering through a psychedelic, ever-dissolving landscape of geometric shapes and shifting colours.
Slow-burn success: by 2008 the track had reached No. 1 on Beatport's chill-out chart, where it stayed for roughly two years.
The parent album peaked at No. 93 on the UK Albums Chart — modest numbers for a record that became an afterparty staple.
Twenty years on, Evelyn re-recorded this at Abbey Road's Studio Two with a gospel choir, string quartet and horns — Mozez himself singing lead.

title: You Wish

description: The first full track on Thought So… (2008), Nightmares on Wax's Leeds-to-Ibiza travelogue album — organ, handclaps and a simple, sunny mantra: the feeling is real, and it's love.

pops.text: After a 38-second intro, this is the first full track on Thought So…, released August 25, 2008 on Warp Records.
Thought So… is a travelogue of an album — AllMusic noted its tracks were recorded in locales ranging from Leeds to Ibiza.
There's a reason it sounds sunnier: Evelyn was in the middle of moving from Leeds to Ibiza, his new home, while making this record.
The whole hook is right there in the lyric: 'the feeling is real and there's love' — repeated like a beach-day mantra.
PopMatters called this the album's first and best song, singling out its organs and funky handclaps.
The writing credits are a band affair — Evelyn alongside Robin Taylor-Firth, Chris Dawkins and other members of the N.O.W. circle.
Guitarist Chris Dawkins, one of those co-writers, was a fixture of the Nightmares on Wax live band.
It doubled as a single: 'Da Feelin' was paired with 'Calling' for a December 2008 release, remixes in tow.
In 2014 it earned a place on N.O.W. Is The Time, the career retrospective marking 25 years of Nightmares on Wax.
Evelyn is Warp Records' longest-serving artist — his first release on the label dates back to 1989.

title: Da Feelin

description: A bright, funky pop gem tucked late on Perpetual Groove's 2004 album All This Everything. One reviewer called it one of the best pop songs to come out of the jam world since the Spin Doctors.

pops.text: Welcome to PGroove! 'Scooter' comes from All This Everything, released September 21, 2004 on Harmonized Records.
Perpetual Groove formed in 1997 in Savannah, Georgia, where the founders met as students at the Savannah College of Art and Design.
At 4 minutes 20 seconds, 'Scooter' is positively compact for a jam band — it's track 11 of the album's 15 songs.
Home Grown Music's review praised its 'Caucasian pop-funk' and called it one of the best pop songs to come out of the jam world since the Spin Doctors.
Bright tune, dark lyric: it opens with Brock Butler singing, 'At first I tried to speculate, but then I asked myself why.'
Butler handles guitar and lead vocals, with Adam Perry on bass — the band's two founding members.
Track data puts 'Scooter' at a danceable 105 BPM in the key of C major, in a straight 4/4 groove.
The classic lineup clicked in 2001, when drummer Albert Suttle and keyboardist Matt McDonald — both then active-duty U.S. Army — joined after a Savannah open-mic night.
Its album is bookended by a theme: All This Everything opens with the 92-second 'Life' and closes with 'And Everything.'
PGroove even hosted their own festival, Amberland, held every Memorial Day weekend — part concert, part family reunion.

title: Scooter

description: A signature groove from Perpetual Groove's 2003 album Sweet Oblivious Antidote, anchored by Adam Perry's opening bass line. In concert it grew into a monster, stretching to nearly 20 minutes live.

pops.text: 'Teakwood Betz' is track 5 of 10 on Sweet Oblivious Antidote, released January 21, 2003 on Harmonized Records.
The studio version already runs about seven and a half minutes — PGroove rarely did anything small.
That slinky opening bass line is Adam Perry's. A reviewer of the band's reunion show said its effect was beyond words.
Live, the song balloons: the version on Sweet Oblivious Antidote (Live) clocks in at 19 minutes 47 seconds.
The parent album's artwork mimics an antique medicine bottle on the outside, with futuristic liner notes inside — old cure, new trip.
Reviewers heard echoes of the Flecktones in the album's 'Astro Monkey' and called tracks like this one 'sublime.'
Perpetual Groove announced an indefinite hiatus in January 2013 — fans feared the groove had stopped for good.
It hadn't! The band reunited in May 2015 at Athens' Georgia Theatre, and 'Teakwood Betz' closed the second set before more than 1,000 loyal fans.
Quietly, the song became a streaming staple for a cult band: it has passed 5 million plays on Spotify.
In January 2023, Sweet Oblivious Antidote got a 20th Anniversary Edition, introducing 'Teakwood Betz' to a new generation of vinyl diggers.

title: Teakwood Betz

description: The first half of the two-part title suite from Perpetual Groove's 2004 album All This Everything. It picks up the album's opening 'Life' theme and launches the record's big, life-sized questions.

pops.text: This is track 2 on All This Everything, released September 21, 2004 — it follows the album's 92-second opener, 'Life.'
Part 2 comes next on the album, running 5:12. Together the two parts form the record's title suite.
The album runs 15 tracks and just under 67 minutes on Harmonized Records — PGroove's second release.
It's 'not quite a concept album,' wrote Home Grown Music, but the musical theme of 'Life' is revisited all the way through.
Fans have a name for this sound: 'trance arena rock' — rock and indie electronica with a touch of metal.
Singer-guitarist Brock Butler's voice drew a comparison in reviews to Dashboard Confessional's Chris Carrabba — minus the whining, the reviewer added.
At a fan-designed setlist show in Atlanta in December 2016, the band opened with 'Life' flowing straight into parts 1 and 2 of this song.
The band formed in Savannah in 1997, then relocated to Athens, Georgia — hometown of R.E.M. and Widespread Panic.
Album acts are a PGroove specialty: on that same Atlanta run, they played their 2007 album LIVELOVEDIE in its entirety the following night.
The album closes with 'And Everything,' bringing the dreamer full circle back to the 'Life' theme where this song began.

title: All This Everything, pt 1

description: Prince and the Revolution's breathless fourth single from Purple Rain, recorded live at Minneapolis's First Avenue in 1983. It peaked at No. 8 and segues on the album straight into 'Baby I'm a Star.'

pops.text: This was the fourth single from Purple Rain, released in the U.S. on November 28, 1984.
Believe it or not, this polished pop hit was recorded live — on August 3, 1983, at First Avenue in Minneapolis.
That First Avenue show was a benefit for the Minnesota Dance Theatre, captured on a mobile recording unit parked outside.
It was also guitarist Wendy Melvoin's live debut with the Revolution — she was just 19 years old.
The album version is barely three minutes long — 2:49 of pure, galloping Minneapolis Sound, driven by Oberheim synth and a Linn drum machine feel.
It peaked at No. 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 in February 1985 — the fourth straight Top 10 single from Purple Rain.
The single's B-side was a gift for collectors: the previously unreleased 'Another Lonely Christmas.'
The 12-inch version stretches to 10:15 — it's actually a rehearsal jam with Sheila E. on percussion, plus Eddie M. on sax and Miko Weaver on guitar.
An even longer jam, nearly 31 minutes, was never officially released — it circulates only as a bootleg.

This official video was filmed live at the Capital Centre in Landover, Maryland, on November 20, 1984. On the album, the song segues straight into 'Baby I'm a Star,' recorded at that same First Avenue night.

title: I Would Die 4 U

description: Prince's career-defining power ballad, recorded live at First Avenue in 1983 and released as the title track of his 1984 album and film. It peaked at No. 2 and became his signature song.

pops.text: 'Purple Rain' was the third single from the album of the same name, released September 26, 1984.
The basic track was recorded live at First Avenue in Minneapolis on August 3, 1983, then overdubbed at Sunset Sound in Los Angeles.
The original live performance ran about 11 minutes. Prince edited it down to 8:41 for the album — and to 4:05 for the single.
Those swelling strings? Lisa Coleman of the Revolution created the string arrangement that was overdubbed in Los Angeles.
Prince worried the song sounded like Journey's 'Faithfully,' so he phoned Journey's Jonathan Cain to play it for him. Cain gave it his blessing.
Prince first conceived it as a country song and asked Stevie Nicks to write the lyrics. Intimidated by the music, she declined — so Prince wrote them himself.
Prince explained the title: blood in the sky makes red plus blue — purple. It's about the end of the world, and letting faith guide you through it with the one you love.
It peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 for two weeks, held off by Wham!'s 'Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go' — though it did top the Cash Box chart.
At Super Bowl XLI in 2007, Prince closed his halftime show with this song — during an actual downpour, under purple lights. It is still ranked among the greatest halftime shows ever.

After Prince's death in 2016, 'Purple Rain' re-entered the Hot 100 at No. 4 and hit No. 1 in France. Rolling Stone ranks it No. 18 on its 500 Greatest Songs of All Time — and it was the last song Prince ever performed live, in Atlanta on April 14, 2016.

title: Purple Rain
